newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says fleet deal sealed, Yeltsin op on track.
newsitem.headline: Russia says fleet deal sealed, Yeltsin op on track.

text.p: The Kremlin on Thursday announced a breakthrough in a long-running row with Ukraine over dividing the Black Sea fleet and said President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation would go ahead as planned.

Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said Yeltsin had cut a "strong, powerful" figure during a meeting at which they discussed the fate of the fleet, but was more cautious than Russian officials on the chances of reaching a final agreement.

"I saw the real Boris Yeltsin -- a strong powerful person who knows what he wants. And the thing he wants now is to have an operation as soon as possible so he can return to the political scene," Kuchma told a news conference.
The two leaders met at the Barvikha sanitorium near Moscow where Yeltsin, 65, is preparing for his operation.
Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said they had reached agreement "on all the questions".

"Before the middle of November it is expected that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will visit Kiev when a number of agreements will be signed on splitting up the fleet, where it will be based and on financing as well," Yastrzhembsky said.
The dispute over the ageing Black Sea fleet of 600 vessels has dragged on since the Soviet Union fell apart in late 1991 and has defied all previous attempts to solve it.

Just before the two leaders met, Russia's state Duma (lower house of parliament) warned Ukraine that Moscow would never hand over control of Sevastopol, the port city in the Crimean peninsula where the fleet is based.
Crimea was long part of Russia but was handed to Ukraine by then Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1954.

"Sevastopol was, is and will be the main naval base of Russia's Black Sea fleet. Unilateral moves by Ukraine to divide it will lead not just to the division but the destruction of the fleet," read the Duma's appeal, which has no legal force.
Yastrzhembsky hinted at possible trouble to come by saying the question of Sevastopol's status had been removed from the agenda rather than confirming the matter had been solved.
Kuchma, mindful that a final deal has proved elusive, told reporters: "We discussed the date (for signing a deal). Alas these dates have changed so many times in the past."
Yeltsin promised Kuchma that his first official visit after he had recovered from his operation would be to Kiev to sign a long-delayed friendship agreement between the two Slav states.
Yastrzhembsky said that preparations for the president's operation were going according to plan. "There is no change to the schedule laid down for the operation," he said.
He said Russian medical specialists had received some equipment from U.S. heart surgery pioneer Michael DeBakey and might use this during the operation.
The president had two heart attacks last year and some doctors say he may have had a third just before the second round of a presidential election last July.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had specifically asked him to deny suggestions made earlier this week by ousted security chief Alexander Lebed that Chernomyrdin would soon be removed.
Western investors view Chernomyrdin as the best guarantor of economic stability in Russia.
The former gas industry boss has insisted his policies will not change although his government is being forced to revise the 1997 budget plans after parliament voted down the draft.
In a further sign of the government's economic difficulties, a Russian official said talks with a visiting mission of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Moscow were proving tricky.
The official said tax collection was the main obstacle in the discussions over whether to release the next tranche of a $10 billion three-year IMF loan to Russia.
